newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: PHILIPS PROFIT WARNING PROMPTS REORGANISATION TALK.
newsitem.headline: PHILIPS PROFIT WARNING PROMPTS REORGANISATION TALK.

text.p: A warning from Philips Electronics NV on Monday that operating profits were unlikely to rise in the second half prompted speculation more reorganisation might be needed at Europe's biggest consumer electronics firm.
The Dutch giant said preliminary information for the third quarter made it "most unlikely" there would be an improvement in operating profit in the second half, causing its shares to dive.
On a broadly-mixed Amsterdam bourse Philips stock dropped over 5.5 percent, or 3.60 guilders, to 61.20 guilders with volume a brisker than normal 4.5 million shares.
"Things are deteriorating even faster than they expected so far. That's the only thing we can say now. The big problems are at the consumer products unit," said ING anlyst Steven Vrolijk.
Analysts said Philips, like its competitors, was trading in tough conditions and, until markets picked up, one way to keep earnings ticking was through tight business controls.

"What they could do is go over every division again. In our opinion it's not only the consumer products division but there are also problems at the professional and systems division which is not making money," said Vrolijk.
"They've got to just keep cutting (costs) everywhere they can. Eventually that will mean fewer jobs in Europe and probably also in the United States," Vrolijk added.

Marc Langeveld at Kempen & Co said the profit warning would turn the focus sharply back onto reorganisation manoeuvres at Philips' third quarter results announcement on October 24, the first set of results to be published since Cor Boonstra took up the chairmanship of Philips on October 1.
He said it was extremely difficult to predict how Philips would reorganise further but expected moderate changes.

"I believe there will be further restructurings. But that's only normal with Boonstra taking up office. He would have done that anyway. It's best to do those things when you just start your new job," said Langeveld.
"It's difficult to forecast. It will be restructurings that take place at a micro-level," said Langeveld.

Philips in July announced job cuts of 6,000 over 18 months from its Sound & Vision unit, struggling with price pressures and disappointing demand for its products, and said outsourcing to lower cost countries would be a key part of restructuring.

London-based Morgan Stanley analyst Angela Dean said the company would have to grit its teeth and concentrate again on controlling inventories and working capital, working on tightening control of purchasing costs.

"There are group-wide things (Philips could concentrate on) like control of inventories and working capital. These seemed to be just going their way in the second quarter but maybe it's gone the wrong way again in the third quarter," she said.
"Maybe they have to do something more aggressive that involves restructuring provisions or costs in areas they haven't talked about so far," said Dean.
Analysts said Philips was not alone in facing sluggish markets and price erosion.
"It's the old story -- price pressure and manufacturers fighting for market share, everything we've seen quite a few times before," said ING' Vrolijk.

"You could say this is a difficult year for them for some reasons that are not of their own making," said Dean. "One thing that will go right for them is that some of the industries they're in are going to pick up," she added.
Analysts had been expecting a slowdown during the third quarter anyway, but some said they would downgrade forecasts in the wake of the warning on operating profits.

Vrolijk said he had been forecasting 1.1 billion guilders net profit from normal operations for the first nine months of 1996. "That has to come down because we were not negative enough for third quarter results."
He said he was now looking for nine month net from normal operations of 969 million guilders, compared to 1.7 billion in the same year-earlier period.
Others said they would seek more information from Philips before changing their forecasts.
